c-mongol-area.text: At its peak the Mongol empire covered some 23 million square km, the largest contiguous land empire in world history.
c-mongol-area.label: approx
c-mongol-area.note: A modern estimate for frontiers that shifted constantly.

c-abulughod.text: Janet Abu-Lughod described a Eurasian 'world system' of about 1250-1350, made possible by the Mongol empire and made of eight overlapping circuits of trade, which plague and other epidemics and the Mongols' loss of China in 1368 helped to break apart.
c-abulughod.label: debated
c-abulughod.note: An influential model, not a settled fact. Her point was that Europe's later dominance was not an 'inherent historical necessity'.

c-secret-history.text: The Secret History of the Mongols, by an unknown 13th-century author, is the main account from the Mongol side.
c-secret-history.label: debated
c-secret-history.note: Its date is uncertain (Britannica gives 1240 with a query). Its early parts cannot be checked against other sources, but historians warn it would be 'unwise to dismiss' it 'as pure fiction'.

c-rashid.text: Rashid al-Din (1247-1318), who came from a Jewish family of Hamadan and converted to Islam, served the Mongol rulers of Iran as vizier and wrote a universal history, the Jami' al-tawarikh, beginning with a history of the Mongols commissioned by Ghazan.
c-rashid.label: consensus

c-ibnbattuta.text: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta saw the Black Death in Syria in 1348.
c-ibnbattuta.label: consensus

c-bd-genome.text: In 2011 scientists reconstructed the genome of the Black Death bacterium, Yersinia pestis, from a London plague cemetery; all the strains that infect humans today descend from it.
c-bd-genome.label: consensus

c-lead-plague.text: Lead pollution in an Alpine ice core fell to natural levels in 1349-53, when the Black Death halted mining and smelting.
c-lead-plague.label: consensus

c-bluerings.text: Unusual 'blue rings' in Pyrenean trees record cold, wet summers in 1345, 1346 and 1347.
c-bluerings.label: approx
c-bluerings.note: Probably the result of a volcanic eruption around 1345; see 12.3.

c-temujin.text: Temüjin, the future Chinggis Khan, may have been born in 1155, 1162 (the date favoured in Mongolia today) or 1167.
c-temujin.label: approx
c-temujin.note: No contemporary record gives the year.

c-kuriltai.text: In 1206 a great assembly by the Onon River proclaimed him Chinggis Khan; the title probably meant 'Universal Ruler'.
c-kuriltai.label: consensus

c-decimal.text: His army was divided on the decimal system, in units of tens.
c-decimal.label: consensus

c-jin.text: He attacked the Jin empire of northern China in 1211 and took Beijing in 1215.
c-jin.label: consensus

c-khwarazm.text: After the governor of Otrar massacred a caravan sent under Mongol protection, Chinggis invaded the Khwarazmian empire; Bukhara, Samarkand and the capital Urgench were taken and sacked in 1220-21.
c-khwarazm.label: consensus

c-merv.text: Merv, an ancient city of Central Asia, was destroyed by the Mongols in 1221 and never regained its former prosperity.
c-merv.label: consensus

c-tolls.text: How many people the conquests killed is unknown.
c-tolls.label: debated
c-tolls.note: A 2014 Iranian study argues the actual 'rate of murder and pillage' was 'much lower' than some historians claim. Reviewing Peter Jackson (2017), Steve Donoghue writes that 'as Jackson readily admits, such reclamation has its limits'; Jackson notes that Nishapur was 'singled out for especially harsh treatment'.

c-may.text: Timothy May calls the Mongols 'the most destructive force in the pre-modern world', yet argues that their rule also had 'stabilizing effects'.
c-may.label: debated
c-may.note: One historian's balance; others weigh the destruction more heavily.

c-baghdad1258.text: In February 1258 Hülegü, a grandson of Chinggis, took Baghdad and killed many of its inhabitants; the execution of the caliph al-Musta'sim left Islam without a caliph for the first time in its history.
c-baghdad1258.label: consensus

c-ainjalut.text: At Ain Jalut in Palestine, on 3 September 1260, the Mamluks of Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol army, halting the westward expansion of the Mongol empire.
c-ainjalut.label: approx

c-ghazan.text: Ghazan, Mongol ruler of Iran, converted from Buddhism to Islam before taking the throne in 1295; Rashid al-Din became his vizier.
c-ghazan.label: consensus

c-goldenhorde.text: The Golden Horde ruled the western steppe from Sarai on the lower Volga. Russian princes, above all those of Moscow, collected its tribute; under Öz Beg (1312-41) the Horde became Muslim, in 1380 Russian princes defeated it at Kulikovo, and its last remnant was destroyed in 1502.
c-goldenhorde.label: consensus

c-yoke.text: The traditional Russian view saw the Mongol conquest as a disaster, the 'Tatar yoke'.
c-yoke.label: debated
c-yoke.note: Reviewing Donald Ostrowski (1998), Will Ryan says he takes the revisionist position 'that after an initial period of deprivation Muscovy for the most part flourished', and finds his case that Muscovy took its 'dual structure' of administration from the Horde 'demonstrated persuasively if not conclusively'. Ostrowski observes that the older view of economic destruction has 'a metahistorical appeal both to Russian nationalists and to Marxist historians'.

c-yoke-term.text: The earliest known use of the phrase 'Tatar yoke' in Slavic writing dates from the second half of the 17th century.
c-yoke-term.label: debated
c-yoke-term.note: Halperin (2025) reports that the earliest known Slavic use, found by Lev Dmitriev, dates from the second half of the 17th century, while Seleznev has found two Latin references from the 13th century. He argues that 'any author familiar with Scripture could easily independently have made the leap from "Yoke" to "Tatar Yoke"'.

c-khubilai.text: Khubilai Khan proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271, ruled from Dadu (Beijing), ended the Song in 1279 and made paper money the sole medium of exchange.
c-khubilai.label: consensus

c-japan.text: Khubilai's invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281 failed; his fleets were virtually annihilated, as much by storms as by Japanese resistance.
c-japan.label: debated
c-japan.note: Chinese records claim 4,400 ships in 1281; the underwater archaeologist Kenzo Hayashida thinks the fleet's size was exaggerated, and found anchors 'only roughly finished'.

c-rubruck.text: The Franciscan William of Rubruck (1253-55) was the first European to visit the Mongol capital, Karakorum, and return to write about it.
c-rubruck.label: consensus

c-sauma.text: Rabban Sauma, a Syriac Christian monk, came to Europe in 1287 for the Mongol ruler of Iran to seek joint action against the Muslims of Palestine, and met the kings of France and England.
c-sauma.label: consensus

c-polo.text: Whether Marco Polo really went to China is debated.
c-polo.label: debated
c-polo.note: Frances Wood asks why his book omits 'tea, foot-binding, or even the Great Wall'; Hans Ulrich Vogel (2013) finds that he alone described 'precisely how paper for money was made' and that his account of salt production 'checks out with Chinese documents'.

c-origin.text: Ancient DNA from graves at Kara-Djigach and Burana in Kyrgyzstan, whose tombstones of 1338-39 record deaths from 'pestilence', contains the plague strain from which the Black Death's lineages branched out, supporting an origin in that region.
c-origin.label: approx
c-origin.note: Spyrou et al. (2022). The Tian Shan region is the strongest candidate, not a proven single source.

c-ibnwardi.text: An Arabic account by Ibn al-Wardi, long used to trace the plague's rapid overland spread, has been argued (2025) to be a literary work that 'should not be taken literally'.
c-ibnwardi.label: debated
c-ibnwardi.note: New, by Muhammed Omar and Nahyan Fancy; they say the 'Quick Transit Theory' built on it is 'severely called into question'.

c-caffa.text: Gabriele de' Mussis wrote that at the siege of Caffa in Crimea (1346) the Mongol army hurled plague-infected corpses into the city.
c-caffa.label: debated
c-caffa.note: Mark Wheelis (2002) finds the story plausible but concludes that plague likely entered Europe from Crimea independently of it.

c-grain.text: Martin Bauch and Ulf Büntgen (2025) argue that a volcanic eruption around 1345 caused cold summers and famine, so that Venice, Genoa and Pisa imported grain from the Golden Horde in 1347, and infected fleas most likely travelled with it.
c-grain.label: debated
c-grain.note: New; the authors present the chain as likely, not proven.

c-bd-europe.text: The Black Death ravaged Europe between 1347 and 1351, taking a proportionally greater toll of life than any earlier epidemic or war.
c-bd-europe.label: consensus

c-mortality.text: Estimates of the share of Europe's population that died range from 30-40 percent (Philip Ziegler) through 40-50 (Robert Gottfried) and 47-48 (Rosemary Horrox) to about 60 percent (Ole Benedictow).
c-mortality.label: debated
c-mortality.note: Paula Arthur (2010) argues for a 'much higher mortality figure' than the older estimates.

c-pollen.text: A 2022 study of 1,634 pollen samples from 261 sites in 19 countries found farming collapsed in Scandinavia, France, south-western Germany, Greece and central Italy, but continued or grew in Ireland, Iberia and much of central and eastern Europe.
c-pollen.label: debated
c-pollen.note: Izdebski et al. It challenges the idea of uniformly high mortality across Europe.

c-dols.text: Michael Dols traced the plague in the Middle East from Arabic sources and found that its recurrences 'appreciably slowed population growth' in Egypt and Syria for a century and a half.
c-dols.label: approx

c-wells.text: As the plague spread, Christians accused Jews of plotting to destroy them by poisoning the wells, an accusation already made in Franconia in 1319.
c-wells.label: consensus

c-strasbourg.text: In Strasbourg in February 1349 the Jews were burned on a wooden platform in their cemetery; the chronicler Jacob von Königshofen says about two thousand died, and that 'the money was indeed the thing that killed the Jews'.
c-strasbourg.label: approx
c-strasbourg.note: The number is the chronicler's. He dates it to St Valentine's Day (14 February); the Jewish Encyclopedia gives 16 February.

c-clement.text: Pope Clement VI issued a bull in 1348 that urged the protection of Jews against the accusation that they had caused the plague by poisoning wells; Königshofen notes that in Avignon 'the pope protected them'.
c-clement.label: consensus

c-jjk-persecution.text: An economic study of city-level data finds that persecution of Jews during the Black Death was less likely where Jews played important economic roles.
c-jjk-persecution.label: debated
c-jjk-persecution.note: A statistical inference by Jedwab, Johnson and Koyama; the Strasbourg chronicle, by contrast, points to debts and money as a motive.

c-flagellants.text: Flagellants, who whipped themselves in public to share in Christ's sufferings, spread with the plague; Pope Clement VI condemned the practice in 1349.
c-flagellants.label: consensus

c-statute.text: England's Ordinance of Labourers (1349) complained that because 'a great part of the people' had died in the pestilence, workers would not serve 'unless they receive excessive wages', and tried to hold wages at pre-plague levels; the Statute of Labourers (1351) had the same aim.
c-statute.label: consensus

c-peasants.text: The English Peasants' Revolt began in Essex in May 1381; the rebels resented the Statute of Labourers, and the young Richard II promised them the abolition of serfdom, a promise not kept.
c-peasants.label: consensus

c-ball.text: The radical priest John Ball is remembered for the couplet 'Whan Adam dalf, and Eve span, / Wo was thanne a gentilman?', 'When Adam dug and Eve spun, who was then a nobleman?'
c-ball.label: tradition
c-ball.note: Attributed to Ball by the chronicler Thomas Walsingham; the modern English is ours, following the Rochester glosses. It uses the Genesis story of the first humans to question inherited rank.

c-serfdom.text: By about 1500 serfdom had virtually disappeared in western Europe, while east of the Elbe a 'second serfdom', harsher than the first, spread from the 15th century.
c-serfdom.label: debated
c-serfdom.note: Why the two halves diverged is debated: Munro notes that population decline hastened serfdom's end in the West, while Robert Brenner attacked 'simplistic economic models of other historians that neglected to consider the dynamics of class relationships and class conflicts'.

c-pamuk.text: Şevket Pamuk finds that after the plague real wages held up best in England and the Low Countries, so that a wage gap opened between north-west Europe and the rest of the continent after 1450.
c-pamuk.label: debated
c-pamuk.note: One influential account of the roots of the 'Great Divergence'.

c-vv.text: Nico Voigtländer and Joachim Voth argue that the Black Death raised wages sharply, and that plague, war and unhealthy cities then kept death rates and incomes high in Europe.
c-vv.label: debated

c-jjk-survey.text: A 2022 survey concludes that the plague raised wages, but that 'in the long run, this rise was only sustained in some parts of Europe'.
c-jjk-survey.label: debated
c-jjk-survey.note: Jedwab, Johnson and Koyama link the plague to the end of western serfdom and to the beginnings of Europe's divergence from other regions.

c-alfani.text: Guido Alfani notes that the Black Death 'is usually believed' to have reduced inequality, but that the record of other epidemics makes the picture 'much more complex'.
c-alfani.label: debated

c-immune.text: A 2022 ancient-DNA study suggests the plague favoured immune-gene variants that protected against it but that today are associated with a higher risk of autoimmune disease.
c-immune.label: debated
c-immune.note: New and still being tested; based on 206 ancient samples from London, checked against Denmark.

c-hyw.text: The Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) was an intermittent conflict between England and France; despite English victories such as Crécy (1346) and Poitiers (1356), by 1453 England held only Calais.
c-hyw.label: consensus

c-joan.text: Joan of Arc raised the siege of Orléans in 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims; tried for witchcraft and heresy, she was burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431, and was canonised in 1920.
c-joan.label: consensus

c-joan-voices.text: Joan said she heard the voices of Saints Michael, Catherine and Margaret.
c-joan-voices.label: tradition
c-joan-voices.note: Her own testimony; believers and historians interpret it in different ways.

c-schism.text: After almost 70 years in which the popes lived at Avignon, the Western Schism (1378-1417) produced two and then three rival popes, until the Council of Constance elected Martin V in November 1417.
c-schism.label: consensus

c-wyclif.text: John Wyclif denied the doctrine of transubstantiation and stressed the primacy of Scripture; his followers, the Lollards, produced the first complete English Bible from 1382, and the Council of Constance condemned him in 1415.
c-wyclif.label: consensus

c-hus.text: The Czech reformer Jan Hus came to Constance on King Sigismund's promise of safe-conduct, was arrested, tried as a follower of Wyclif and burned on 6 July 1415.
c-hus.label: debated
c-hus.note: The events are agreed; how far his ideas depended on Wyclif rather than on a Czech reform movement is debated.

c-petrarch.text: Petrarch (1304-1374), crowned poet laureate in Rome in 1341, hunted for lost classical texts and found Cicero's letters to Atticus at Verona.
c-petrarch.label: consensus

c-medici.text: Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici (1360-1429) founded the Medici bank and in 1422 became banker to the papacy; his son Cosimo dominated Florence from 1434.
c-medici.label: consensus

c-gutenberg.text: The Gutenberg Bible (Mainz, c. 1455) was the first book printed with movable metal type in western Europe, about 180 copies; Korean printers had used movable metal type about a century earlier.
c-gutenberg.label: consensus

c-partidas.text: The Siete Partidas, a law code begun under Alfonso X of Castile (1221-1284), was recognised as a body of law at the Cortes of Alcalá de Henares in 1348 and influenced the law of some of Spain's former colonies.
c-partidas.label: consensus

c-1391.text: In June 1391 Christian mobs attacked the Jews of Seville, killing thousands and forcing others into baptism; the violence spread across Castile, Aragon and Mallorca.
c-1391.label: approx
c-1391.note: The number killed is not known precisely. Those baptised and their descendants became known as conversos.

c-1391-view.text: Historians once saw 1391 as the moment when 'centuries of coexistence gave way to expulsion and inquisition'.
c-1391-view.label: debated
c-1391-view.note: Recent work, such as Paola Tartakoff's, finds conflict over conversion earlier; compare the convivencia debate in 11.2.

c-tortosa.text: At the Disputation of Tortosa (1413-14), called by the antipope Benedict XIII, the convert Gerónimo de Santa Fe argued from Jewish texts that the Messiah had come; it ran to 69 sessions and many conversions followed.
c-tortosa.label: approx
c-tortosa.note: The Encyclopaedia Judaica calls it 'a propagandist missionary attack accompanied by psychological pressure'.

c-isabella.text: Isabella of Castile married Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469 and became queen of Castile in 1474; from 1479 the two crowns were united in their persons.
c-isabella.label: consensus

c-inquisition.text: In 1478 Pope Sixtus IV authorised the Spanish Inquisition, which held its first auto de fe in Seville in February 1481; under Tomás de Torquemada about 2,000 people were burned.
c-inquisition.label: approx
c-inquisition.note: The figure for Torquemada's time is Britannica's estimate.

c-granada.text: Muhammad XII surrendered Granada to Ferdinand and Isabella on 2 January 1492, ending Muslim rule in Spain.
c-granada.label: consensus

c-alhambra.text: The Alhambra Decree of 31 March 1492 ordered the Jews of Ferdinand and Isabella's kingdoms to leave by the end of July, blaming the 'interaction between the Jews and these Christians', the conversos.
c-alhambra.label: consensus

c-expelled.text: How many Jews left Spain is debated: estimates run from 40,000-50,000 to 150,000-200,000.
c-expelled.label: debated
c-expelled.note: Gretchen Starr-LeBeau, drawing on Henry Kamen, suggests 40,000-50,000 and notes that 'most converted rather than emigrated'; Luis Suárez gave 100,000; a French university course says most historians estimate 150,000-200,000.

c-alhambra-memory.text: Spain declared the decree without effect in 1968, and under a 2015 law 72,199 people with Sephardic Jewish ancestry had been granted Spanish citizenship by the end of 2024.
c-alhambra-memory.label: consensus

c-henry.text: Prince Henry 'the Navigator' of Portugal (1394-1460) helped his father capture Ceuta in Morocco in 1415 and sponsored voyages to Madeira and down the coast of Africa.
c-henry.label: consensus

c-timur.text: Timur (1336-1405), a conqueror from Central Asia, massacred the populations of whole cities in Iran, invaded India in 1398 and died at Otrar at the start of a campaign against China.
c-timur.label: consensus

c-samarkand.text: Samarkand was the capital of the Timurid realm, and Timur strove to make it the most splendid city in Asia; the city's main growth came in the Timurid period (14th-15th centuries), and its monuments include the Registan, the Bibi-Khanum mosque, the Gur-Emir mausoleum and Ulugh Beg's observatory.
c-samarkand.label: consensus

c-ankara.text: At Ankara on 20 July 1402 Timur defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I, the only Ottoman ruler ever captured by an enemy; a civil war among his sons followed until 1413.
c-ankara.label: consensus

c-osman.text: Osman emerged after 1293 as ruler of a small principality in north-western Anatolia; his son Orhan took Bursa in 1324 or 1326, and from 1354 Orhan's son Süleyman made Gallipoli a permanent base for expansion into Europe.
c-osman.label: approx
c-osman.note: Britannica notes that some sources date Bursa's fall to 1326.

c-gaza.text: Why the Ottomans grew so fast is debated.
c-gaza.label: debated
c-gaza.note: Paul Wittek's thesis that they were driven by gaza, holy war against Christians, faced severe criticism from the 1980s that left it 'largely undermined' (Anis Mahmoud, 2019, whose bibliography includes Rudi Lindner, 1983, and Heath Lowry, 2003).

c-devsirme.text: Under the devshirme, Christian boys from the Balkan provinces were periodically conscripted and converted to Islam; the ablest were trained for government and the rest joined the Janissaries.
c-devsirme.label: consensus

c-1453.text: Mehmed II took Constantinople on 29 May 1453 with perhaps 75,000-100,000 men against about 8,000 defenders; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting, and Hagia Sophia was turned into a mosque.
c-1453.label: approx
c-1453.note: Troop numbers are estimates. Britannica notes that 1453 is widely quoted as the end of the European Middle Ages.

c-mehmed.text: Mehmed II saw himself as heir both of the Roman Caesars and the champion of Islam, and had the Orthodox patriarch Gennadios write a statement of the Christian faith for him.
c-mehmed.label: consensus

c-hagiasophia.text: In 2020 Turkey's highest administrative court cancelled the 1934 decision that had made Hagia Sophia a museum, and it reopened for Muslim worship.
c-hagiasophia.label: debated
c-hagiasophia.note: Supporters said it would 'better reflect Turkey's status as an overwhelmingly Muslim country'; UNESCO said it 'deeply regrets the decision', and Greece called it an 'open provocation'.

c-sundiata.text: Sundiata (died 1255) founded the empire of Mali; Britannica dates his decisive victory over the Susu ruler Sumanguru to 1230.
c-sundiata.label: approx
c-sundiata.note: The dates come from later sources.

c-sunjata-epic.text: Most of what is told about Sundiata comes from an oral epic, recorded in many versions since the late 19th century; the earliest written mention is by Ibn Khaldun in the late 14th century.
c-sunjata-epic.label: debated
c-sunjata-epic.note: David Conrad: 'Some themes are obviously mythical, while others could have a historical basis but cannot be independently confirmed.' Some scholars read the epic chiefly as literature, others as a historical source to set beside documents and archaeology.

c-musa.text: Mansa Musa of Mali made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, and in Cairo he spent so much gold that its value there fell.
c-musa.label: approx
c-musa.note: His reign is dated from 1307 or 1312; Britannica says the Cairo gold market had not fully recovered some years later.

c-musa-mosques.text: Musa had the scholar and architect al-Sahili build mosques at Gao and Timbuktu, and the Sankore mosque at Timbuktu became a centre of teaching.
c-musa-mosques.label: consensus

c-musa-wealth.text: Popular claims that Musa was the wealthiest person who ever lived cannot be checked.
c-musa-wealth.label: debated
c-musa-wealth.note: The Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows him holding a gold coin, and a curator describes him as having 'unlimited access to wealth'; no record allows a modern money value.

c-timbuktu.text: Timbuktu was an intellectual and spiritual capital of Islam in Africa, at its height in the 15th and 16th centuries, with three great mosques: Djingareyber, Sankore and Sidi Yahia.
c-timbuktu.label: consensus

c-timbuktu-mss.text: Manuscripts from more than 30 family libraries in Timbuktu were moved to Bamako in about 1,400 metal boxes; armed groups occupied the city from April 2012 until January 2013.
c-timbuktu-mss.label: consensus

c-songhai.text: Mali lost Timbuktu to the Tuareg and its power to Songhay, whose ruler Sonni Ali drove the Tuareg from Timbuktu and in 1473 took Djenné.
c-songhai.label: approx
c-songhai.note: Britannica's pages give 1431 and 1433 for the Tuareg capture of Timbuktu.

c-gz.text: Great Zimbabwe, built by the Shona between the 11th and 15th centuries, was an important trading centre.
c-gz.label: approx
c-gz.note: UNESCO dates the site to 1100-1450 and the Great Enclosure to the 14th century; on its beginnings see 11.9.

c-kilwa2.text: Kilwa was at its height in the 13th and 14th centuries; Ibn Battuta, who visited in 1331-32, called it one of the most beautiful cities of the world.
c-kilwa2.label: consensus

c-solomonid.text: In 1270 Yekuno Amlak took the throne of Ethiopia, founding a dynasty that claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba through their son Menilek.
c-solomonid.label: tradition
c-solomonid.note: The accession is historical; the descent is the dynasty's claim.

c-kebra.text: The Kebra Nagast, written in the early 14th century, tells how Menilek, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, brought the Ark of the Covenant to Aksum.
c-kebra.label: tradition
c-kebra.note: Britannica calls it 'a combination of mythical history, allegory, and apocalypse'. The Queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon is in 1 Kings 10; Menilek and the Ark story come from Ethiopian tradition.

c-benin.text: Edo tradition traces Benin's royal line to a prince from Ife; Ewuare (reigned c. 1440-80) greatly enlarged the kingdom.
c-benin.label: tradition
c-benin.note: Ewuare's reign is approximate; the founding story is tradition.

c-kongo.text: The kingdom of Kongo was traditionally founded around 1390; the Portuguese arrived in 1483, and in 1491 its king, Nzinga a Nkuwu, and his son were baptised.
c-kongo.label: tradition
c-kongo.note: The founding date is traditional; the baptism is recorded.

c-hongwu.text: Zhu Yuanzhang, born a poor peasant in 1328, rose through the rebellions against the Mongols and reigned as the Hongwu emperor, founder of the Ming, from 1368 to 1398.
c-hongwu.label: consensus

c-redturbans.text: The Red Turbans, peasant rebels of the mid-14th century who regarded their leader as an incarnation of the bodhisattva Maitreya, rose against the Yuan; their rebellion was put down, but rival rebel forces under Zhu Yuanzhang toppled the dynasty.
c-redturbans.label: approx
c-redturbans.note: Zhu first served in a Red Turban army; Britannica treats his later forces as a rival movement.

c-yongle.text: The Yongle emperor seized the throne in 1402, moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing and rebuilt it with the Forbidden City.
c-yongle.label: consensus

c-zhenghe.text: Between 1405 and 1433 the eunuch admiral Zheng He led seven voyages; the first carried some 27,800 men on 317 ships, and the fleets reached Calicut, Hormuz and East Africa.
c-zhenghe.label: approx
c-zhenghe.note: The figures come from Chinese records.

c-zhenghe-why.text: The voyages displayed Ming power and brought foreign rulers into the tribute system, adding legitimacy to an emperor who had seized the throne.
c-zhenghe-why.label: debated
c-zhenghe-why.note: An old story that they were a search for the deposed emperor Jianwen is one 'most historians discredit'.

c-shipsize.text: Chinese texts give the largest treasure ships lengths of about 117-149 m; whether wooden ships that big could be built is debated.
c-shipsize.label: debated
c-shipsize.note: Joseph Needham, Louise Levathes and Edward Dreyer accepted the figures; Sleeswyk, Wake and Church judged them impossible. A 2026 review suggests 60-76 m.

c-zhenghe-end.text: The voyages ended amid concern about their high cost, fuelled by the objections of Confucian scholar-officials.
c-zhenghe-end.label: debated
c-zhenghe-end.note: Yang Wei's account; the decision has been explained in several ways.

c-hangul.text: King Sejong of Korea completed an alphabet of 28 letters in 1443 and proclaimed it in 1446, because Chinese characters were not suitable for writing Korean and common people could not record their thoughts.
c-hangul.label: consensus

c-ashikaga.text: In Japan the Ashikaga shoguns ruled from Kyoto from the 1330s, but their power was relatively weak from the outset, and as time passed the office of shogun became increasingly impotent; the Ōnin War was fought in 1467-77.
c-ashikaga.label: consensus

c-khaljis.text: Under the Khalji sultans (1290-1320) the Delhi Sultanate became an imperial power, repelling Mongol attacks and making the southern kingdoms its vassals.
c-khaljis.label: consensus

c-tughluq.text: Muhammad bin Tughluq (reigned 1325-51) moved his capital to Daulatabad in the Deccan and issued coins of base metal with the face value of silver, an experiment that 'failed dismally'.
c-tughluq.label: consensus

c-tughluq-view.text: Muhammad bin Tughluq's reputation is disputed.
c-tughluq-view.label: debated
c-tughluq-view.note: Britannica calls him 'controversial and enigmatic' and his measures 'neither vicious nor visionary'. Ibn Battuta, who served him as grand qadi of Delhi, described him with what Britannica calls 'mixed feelings of terror and sympathy'.

c-timur-delhi.text: Timur's invasion of 1398-99 shattered the power of the Delhi Sultanate in north India.
c-timur-delhi.label: consensus

c-vijayanagara.text: Vijayanagara was founded in 1336 by the Sangama brothers; UNESCO calls its capital, Hampi, the 'last capital of the last great Hindu Kingdom'.
c-vijayanagara.label: consensus

c-bahmani.text: The Bahmani sultanate, founded in 1347 by rebels against Delhi, fought Vijayanagara almost continually over the fertile Raichur doab.
c-bahmani.label: consensus

c-calicut.text: Under its rulers, the Zamorins, Calicut on the Malabar coast became a great port of the Indian Ocean, where Arab merchants bought pepper and ginger and Chinese treasure ships called in the 15th century.
c-calicut.label: consensus

c-melaka.text: Melaka, founded around 1400 by Parameswara, became a tributary of Ming China, and by the 1430s it was the leading commercial emporium of Southeast Asia.
c-melaka.label: approx
c-melaka.note: Britannica says its ruler became a Muslim, taking the name Iskandar Shah, in 1414; whether this was Parameswara himself or his son is uncertain.

c-tenochtitlan.text: The Mexica (Aztecs) founded Tenochtitlan around 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco; by 1519 Britannica estimates it held some 400,000 people.
c-tenochtitlan.label: approx
c-tenochtitlan.note: 1325 is the traditional date; population estimates vary.

c-triple.text: Under Itzcoatl (1428-40) Tenochtitlan allied with Texcoco and Tlacopan in the Triple Alliance, which collected tribute from conquered regions according to what each produced.
c-triple.label: consensus

c-aztec-sacrifice.text: In Aztec religion human sacrifice, particularly by offering a victim's heart to Tonatiuh, was commonly practised, as was bloodletting.
c-aztec-sacrifice.label: consensus

c-tzompantli.text: The Huey Tzompantli, a great skull rack excavated in Mexico City from 2015, was built in stages between 1486 and 1502; of the skulls studied, 60 percent were men, 38 percent women and 2 percent children.
c-tzompantli.label: approx
c-tzompantli.note: Figures from INAH's 2023 study; work continues.

c-sacrifice-scale.text: The scale of Aztec human sacrifice is debated.
c-sacrifice-scale.label: debated
c-sacrifice-scale.note: Many historians once dismissed Spanish reports as exaggerated propaganda; archaeology now confirms sacrifice on a large scale, but not the largest Spanish figures, such as Diego Durán's 80,400 victims at one temple dedication. Caroline Dodds Pennock questions the 'sensationalism' that has hindered 'impartial and empathetic' study of it.

c-pachacuti.text: Pachacuti, Inca ruler from 1438, began the rapid expansion of the Inca empire; tradition credits him with the plan of Cuzco.
c-pachacuti.label: approx
c-pachacuti.note: Britannica gives his reign as 1438-71; the plan of Cuzco is one he 'is said to have devised'.

c-qhapaq.text: The Inca road system, the Qhapaq Ñan, ran some 30,000 km through six modern countries and reached its greatest extent in the 15th century.
c-qhapaq.label: approx
c-qhapaq.note: UNESCO's figure for the whole network.

c-khipu.text: Inca records were kept on khipus, knotted cords; in 2017 researchers matched six khipus to a Spanish census of 1670, a partial reading rather than a full decipherment.
c-khipu.label: debated

c-khipu2025.text: A 2025 study found that one khipu's main cord was made of human hair from someone with a commoner's diet, suggesting commoners took part in making khipus.
c-khipu2025.label: debated
c-khipu2025.note: New; based on a single khipu.

c-chanchan.text: Chan Chan, capital of the Chimú kingdom on Peru's coast, the largest earthen city of the pre-Columbian Americas, reached its height in the 15th century, not long before it fell to the Incas.
c-chanchan.label: consensus

c-pop1492.text: Estimates of the population of the Americas in 1492 range from about 54 million (William Denevan) to 112 million (Henry Dobyns); a 2019 synthesis gives 60.5 million, with a middle range of 44.8-78.2 million.
c-pop1492.label: debated
c-pop1492.note: Koch et al. (2019). Early-20th-century estimates were much lower. The collapse after 1492 is told in Chapter 13.

pages.title: The Mongols and the Black Death
pages.lede: In the 13th century the Mongols built the largest contiguous land empire in history. Their rule linked China, Iran, Russia and the Middle East, and in the 14th century a plague from the steppe killed a large part of the population from Europe to Egypt. This chapter follows both stories and the worlds that recovered afterwards.
body: Chinggis Khan and his heirs conquered an empire of some 23 million square km. [[c-mongol-area]] Janet Abu-Lughod argued that Mongol rule tied Eurasia into a single 'world system' of trade, and that plague and the Mongols' loss of China helped break it apart; Europe's later dominance, she argued, was no historical necessity. [[c-abulughod]]

Our sources come from every side. The Secret History of the Mongols gives the Mongols' own view; [[c-secret-history]] Rashid al-Din, a convert from Judaism who served the Mongol rulers of Iran, wrote their history from within their court; [[c-rashid]] and the traveller Ibn Battuta saw the plague at first hand in Syria. [[c-ibnbattuta]]

Science now adds evidence no chronicler could. Ancient DNA has identified the Black Death's cause, [[c-bd-genome]] lead in Alpine ice shows mining stopping as the plague struck, [[c-lead-plague]] and tree rings record the cold summers that came just before it. [[c-bluerings]]

What it shows

practice.q: Which evidence most directly identifies the cause of the Black Death?
choices: Yersinia pestis DNA from a London plague cemetery
Ibn Battuta's eyewitness account of plague in Syria
The fall in lead in an Alpine ice core in 1349-53
Blue rings in Pyrenean trees from 1345 to 1347
practice.why: In 2011 scientists reconstructed the bacterium's genome from a London plague cemetery: a recovered genome identifies the pathogen itself.

wrong.1: He saw the Black Death in Syria in 1348, but a traveller's account cannot identify a microbe.
wrong.2: The lead record shows that mining and smelting stopped, not which disease stopped them.
wrong.3: The blue rings record cold, wet summers before the plague, not its cause.

practice.q: What did Janet Abu-Lughod's 'world system' model mainly challenge?
choices: The idea that Europe's later dominance was inevitable
The idea that the Mongol empire made Eurasian trade possible
The idea that plague helped break up Eurasian trade
The idea that trade circuits linked Europe and China
practice.why: She described a Eurasian trading system of about 1250-1350, made possible by Mongol rule, and argued that Europe's later dominance was not an 'inherent historical necessity'.

wrong.1: Her model holds that the system was made possible by the Mongol empire.
wrong.2: She herself linked the system's breakdown to plague and other epidemics.
wrong.3: Her eight overlapping circuits of trade are exactly such links.

pages.title: Chinggis Khan and the conquests
pages.lede: A Mongol chief named Temüjin united the peoples of the steppe, took the title Chinggis Khan and led his armies into China and Central Asia. Within two decades he had destroyed some of the great cities of the Islamic world. How to weigh that destruction against what followed is still argued over.
body: Temüjin's birth year is uncertain. [[c-temujin]] In 1206 a great assembly proclaimed him Chinggis Khan, [[c-kuriltai]] and he organised his army in units of tens. [[c-decimal]] He attacked the Jin dynasty of northern China in 1211 and took Beijing in 1215. [[c-jin]]

Then he turned west. When a governor of the Khwarazmian empire massacred a caravan sent under his protection, Chinggis invaded; Bukhara, Samarkand and Urgench were sacked, [[c-khwarazm]] and Merv was destroyed and never recovered its old prosperity. [[c-merv]] He died in 1227. [[c-death1227]]
Chroniclers recorded enormous slaughter, but no one can count the dead, [[c-tolls]] and historians disagree about how to balance the empire's destruction against the order it later imposed. [[c-may]]

practice.q: Why do historians treat the enormous death tolls in medieval accounts of the Mongol conquests with caution?
choices: The deaths cannot be checked, and one study finds fewer
The Mongols left Bukhara and Samarkand largely intact
Merv recovered its old prosperity within a decade
Excavations have since produced exact counts of the dead
practice.why: The destruction is not in doubt; its scale is. No one can count the dead, and a 2014 Iranian study argues the actual 'rate of murder and pillage' was 'much lower' than some historians claim.

wrong.1: Bukhara, Samarkand and Urgench were taken and sacked in 1220-21.
wrong.2: Merv was destroyed in 1221 and never regained its former prosperity.
wrong.3: How many people the conquests killed is unknown; no one can count the dead.

practice.q: What provoked Chinggis Khan's war on the Khwarazmian empire?
choices: Otrar's governor massacred a Mongol-protected caravan
Khwarazm's seizure of Beijing from the Jin in 1215
The sack of a Mongol caravan by the people of Merv
A Khwarazmian army's invasion of the Mongols' homeland
practice.why: After the governor of Otrar massacred a caravan sent under Mongol protection, Chinggis invaded: the war in the west began with an attack on traders.

wrong.1: Beijing was taken by the Mongols themselves, from the Jin, in 1215.
wrong.2: The caravan was massacred by the governor of Otrar; Merv was destroyed later, in 1221.
wrong.3: The war began with the massacre of a caravan at Otrar, after which Chinggis invaded Khwarazm.

pages.title: The khanates and the Pax Mongolica
pages.lede: Chinggis Khan's descendants divided his empire. One sacked Baghdad and killed its Abbasid caliph, another ruled the Russian lands from the steppe, and Khubilai Khan made himself emperor of China. Under Mongol rule merchants, monks and envoys crossed Eurasia, and some wrote about what they saw.
body: In 1258 Hülegü sacked Baghdad and put to death al-Musta'sim, the last Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, [[c-baghdad1258]] but two years later the Mamluks of Egypt stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut. [[c-ainjalut]] Hülegü's descendants ruled Iran, and one of them, Ghazan, became a Muslim in 1295. [[c-ghazan]]

On the western steppe the Golden Horde ruled the Russian principalities through their own princes, who collected its tribute. [[c-goldenhorde]] Russian tradition remembers this as the 'Tatar yoke', a view historians have challenged, [[c-yoke]] and the phrase itself appears in Slavic writing only in the later 17th century, although Latin writers used it as early as the 13th. [[c-yoke-term]]

In China, Khubilai founded the Yuan dynasty and completed the conquest of the Song, [[c-khubilai]] though his invasions of Japan failed. [[c-japan]] Travellers crossed the empire in both directions: the friar William of Rubruck reached Karakorum, [[c-rubruck]] the monk Rabban Sauma travelled to Europe for the Mongol ruler of Iran, [[c-sauma]] and Marco Polo described the court of Khubilai, though whether he really went there is debated. [[c-polo]]

Ruled
Notable

practice.q: What does Donald Ostrowski's revision of the 'Tatar yoke' mainly argue?
choices: Muscovy mostly flourished and borrowed from the Horde
The Horde took no tribute from the Russian princes
The Horde converted the Russian princes to Islam
The yoke ruined Muscovy, as Marxist historians had held
practice.why: His reviewer, Will Ryan, says he argues 'that after an initial period of deprivation Muscovy for the most part flourished', and that it took its 'dual structure' of administration from the Horde.

wrong.1: Russian princes, above all those of Moscow, collected tribute for the Horde.
wrong.2: The Horde itself became Muslim under Öz Beg; the Rus' did not.
wrong.3: That is the older view; Ostrowski notes its appeal to Russian nationalists and Marxist historians.

practice.q: Which evidence best supports Hans Ulrich Vogel's view that Marco Polo really was in China?
choices: His exact account of paper money and salt making
His careful description of the Great Wall's course
His account of tea-drinking and foot-binding
Chinese court records that name him as an official
practice.why: Vogel finds that Polo alone described 'precisely how paper for money was made', and that his account of salt production 'checks out with Chinese documents'.

wrong.1: His book does not mention the Great Wall, one of Frances Wood's arguments against him.
wrong.2: Wood points out that his book mentions neither tea nor foot-binding.
wrong.3: Vogel's case rests on Polo's descriptions checking out against Chinese documents, not on records naming him.

pages.title: The Black Death
pages.lede: In the 1340s a plague reached the Mediterranean from the steppe and spread across Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. Ancient DNA has confirmed its cause and probable origin, but how it travelled and how many it killed are still being worked out.
body: Graves in Kyrgyzstan dated 1338-39 have yielded the strain of plague from which the pandemic's lineages branched out. [[c-origin]] How it reached the Black Sea is less clear: one Arabic account of its rapid spread may be literature rather than report, [[c-ibnwardi]] and the famous story of corpses hurled into besieged Caffa may not explain its arrival in Europe. [[c-caffa]] A new hypothesis links its arrival to grain shipped to Italy after a volcanic eruption and failed harvests. [[c-grain]]

Between 1347 and 1351 the plague killed a larger share of Europe's people than any earlier epidemic or war. [[c-bd-europe]] Estimates of how large a share range from about a third to about 60 percent, [[c-mortality]] and pollen evidence suggests some regions lost far more than others. [[c-pollen]]
The plague also struck the Islamic world. In Egypt and Syria it kept returning, and its recurrences slowed population growth for a century and a half. [[c-dols]]

practice.q: What does the 2022 pollen study most directly imply about a single figure such as Benedictow's 60 percent?
choices: One European figure hides big regional differences
Benedictow's 60 percent applies evenly across Europe
Mortality was highest in Ireland and in Iberia
It proves Ziegler's 30-40 percent was too low
practice.why: Pollen shows farming collapsing in Scandinavia, France, south-western Germany, Greece and central Italy, but continuing or growing in Ireland, Iberia and much of central and eastern Europe.

wrong.1: The study challenges the idea of uniformly high mortality across Europe.
wrong.2: Farming continued or grew in Ireland and Iberia.
wrong.3: The pollen study shows regional variation; it does not settle the overall figure.

practice.q: Why are the gravestones of 1338-39 in Kyrgyzstan important?
choices: They date and place the plague's parent strain
They prove the Mongols hurled corpses at Caffa
They record the first plague deaths in Europe
They show the plague began in southern China
practice.why: Their graves contain the plague strain from which the Black Death's lineages branched out, and the tombstones date the deaths: dated inscriptions plus a genome point to Central Asia.

wrong.1: Caffa is in Crimea, and its story rests on Gabriele de' Mussis's written account.
wrong.2: Kyrgyzstan is in Central Asia; Europe's epidemic began in 1347.
wrong.3: The Tian Shan region of Central Asia is the strongest candidate for the origin.

pages.title: After the plague
pages.lede: The Black Death left behind terror and opportunity. Jews were massacred as scapegoats, penitents whipped themselves in the streets, and the survivors, now scarce, demanded higher wages. Economists still argue over whether the plague set western Europe on a different path from the rest of the world.
body: Panic sought culprits. Jews were accused of poisoning the wells, [[c-wells]] and in town after town they were killed: in Strasbourg the chronicler wrote that 'the money was indeed the thing that killed the Jews'. [[c-strasbourg]] The pope condemned the accusation, [[c-clement]] and one modern study suggests persecution was less likely where Jews were economically important. [[c-jjk-persecution]] Bands of flagellants, too, alarmed the Church. [[c-flagellants]]

With so many dead, labour was scarce and wages rose. England tried to freeze them by law, [[c-statute]] and resentment helped spark the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, [[c-peasants]] whose preacher John Ball questioned the very idea of nobility. [[c-ball]] Over the following century serfdom faded in the West but hardened in the East. [[c-serfdom]]

Did the plague make the West rich? Pamuk traces a wage gap between north-west Europe and the rest after 1450; [[c-pamuk]] Voigtländer and Voth argue high death rates kept incomes high; [[c-vv]] a recent survey finds the gains lasted only in some places, [[c-jjk-survey]] and the plague's effect on inequality is less simple than once thought. [[c-alfani]] Ancient DNA suggests it may even have left a mark on our immune systems. [[c-immune]]

Argument

practice.q: Which finding best supports the view that the plague's long-run economic effects depended on local conditions?
choices: England and the Low Countries kept their high real wages
Wages rose and then stayed high across the whole continent
The Statute of Labourers held English wages at old levels
Serfdom strengthened equally in western and eastern Europe
practice.why: Pamuk finds real wages held up best in England and the Low Countries, opening a gap after 1450, and a 2022 survey finds the rise 'only sustained in some parts of Europe'.

wrong.1: Jedwab, Johnson and Koyama find the rise was 'only sustained in some parts of Europe'.
wrong.2: The law tried to hold wages down, but Pamuk finds English real wages among those that held up best.
wrong.3: Serfdom faded in the West while a 'second serfdom' spread east of the Elbe.

practice.q: What does the Strasbourg chronicle suggest about the motives for the massacre of 1349?
choices: Debts and Jewish property played a central part
The killings were ordered by the pope at Avignon
Most of Strasbourg's Jews had already died of plague
Flagellants carried out the killings on papal orders
practice.why: The chronicler wrote that 'the money was indeed the thing that killed the Jews'.

wrong.1: The chronicle says the pope protected the Jews in Avignon, and Clement VI condemned the poisoning accusation.
wrong.2: The chronicle describes Jews being burned, about two thousand of them, not dying of disease.
wrong.3: Clement VI condemned the flagellants in 1349.

pages.title: Late medieval Latin Europe
pages.lede: England and France fought for over a century, the Church split between rival popes, and reformers challenged its teachings. In Italy, scholars hunted for lost classical texts and bankers grew rich, and in Mainz a new way of printing began.
body: The Hundred Years' War ended with England almost expelled from France. [[c-hyw]] In its course a young woman, Joan of Arc, raised the siege of Orléans, [[c-joan]] saying that saints had spoken to her. [[c-joan-voices]]

The papacy, long resident at Avignon, split between rival popes until the Council of Constance restored a single one in 1417. [[c-schism]] The same council condemned the English theologian John Wyclif, whose followers translated the Bible into English, [[c-wyclif]] and sentenced the Czech reformer Jan Hus, who had come on King Sigismund's promise of safe-conduct; he was burned at the stake. [[c-hus]]

In Italy, Petrarch searched monasteries for lost classical texts, [[c-petrarch]] and in 1422 the Florentine banker Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici became banker to the papacy. [[c-medici]] Around 1455 Johannes Gutenberg printed the Bible at Mainz, the start of a revolution covered in Chapter 13. [[c-gutenberg]]

head: Year
Event
rows: Joan of Arc: Orléans to Rouen

practice.q: What did the Council of Constance (1414-18) achieve for the Church?
choices: It ended the Western Schism by electing Martin V
It moved the papacy back to Avignon from Rome
It approved Wyclif's teaching and English Bible
It sent Jan Hus home under Sigismund's safe-conduct
practice.why: After two and then three rival popes, the council elected Martin V in November 1417: a council resolved what rival popes could not.

wrong.1: The schism followed almost 70 years of popes at Avignon; Constance ended the schism.
wrong.2: Constance condemned Wyclif in 1415.
wrong.3: Hus came on that promise but was arrested, tried and burned on 6 July 1415.

practice.q: Which statement about the Gutenberg Bible is accurate?
choices: The first book from movable metal type in western Europe
The first book ever printed with movable metal type
Printed in Florence and paid for by the Medici bank
Printed as a single copy, for the pope at Rome
practice.why: Printed at Mainz in about 1455, in about 180 copies, it was the first book printed with movable metal type in western Europe.

wrong.1: Korean printers had used movable metal type about a century earlier.
wrong.2: It was printed at Mainz.
wrong.3: About 180 copies were printed.

pages.title: Iberia, 1250 to 1492
pages.lede: After Las Navas de Tolosa (see 11.3), Castile and Aragon came to share one royal couple from 1479, though each kept its own government. Their Jews suffered mass violence and forced conversion in 1391. In 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada and expelled the Jews who would not be baptised, and Portugal had already begun to sail down the coast of Africa.
body: Alfonso X of Castile began a law code, the Siete Partidas, that shaped law in Spain and later in some of its former colonies. [[c-partidas]] In 1391 mobs in Seville and across the kingdoms killed thousands of Jews and forced others to convert, [[c-1391]] a turning point whose meaning historians now debate. [[c-1391-view]] Further pressure followed, as at the Disputation of Tortosa. [[c-tortosa]]

The marriage of Isabella and Ferdinand in 1469 led to the union of the crowns of Castile and Aragon in 1479. [[c-isabella]] Suspicion of the conversos led to the Spanish Inquisition, [[c-inquisition]] and in 1492, three months after Granada surrendered, [[c-granada]] the monarchs ordered the Jews to leave, blaming their influence on the conversos. [[c-alhambra]] How many left is uncertain, [[c-expelled]] and modern Spain has revoked the decree and offered citizenship to descendants. [[c-alhambra-memory]]
Portugal, meanwhile, turned outward: its princes took Ceuta in Morocco in 1415 and explored the Atlantic coast of Africa. [[c-henry]] The voyages of 1492 and after belong to Chapter 13.

head: Estimate of Jews leaving Spain, 1492
Who
rows: Gretchen Starr-LeBeau, drawing on Henry Kamen
'most contemporary historians', per a French university course

practice.q: Why do estimates of the number of Jews who left Spain in 1492 vary so widely?
choices: Historians differ on how many chose baptism instead
Historians agree on 40,000 but disagree on the dates
The decree was annulled before most Jews could leave
Spain's 2015 law gives 72,199 as the number expelled
practice.why: Estimates run from 40,000-50,000 to 150,000-200,000; Gretchen Starr-LeBeau, drawing on Henry Kamen, notes that 'most converted rather than emigrated'.

wrong.2: Its deadline was the end of July 1492; Spain declared it without effect only in 1968.
wrong.3: 72,199 is the number granted Spanish citizenship under that law by the end of 2024.

practice.q: Which link between events is best supported?
choices: Suspicion of conversos shaped Inquisition and expulsion
The attacks of 1391 began in newly conquered Granada
The Inquisition targeted unbaptised Jews, not conversos
Alfonso X's Siete Partidas ordered the expulsion of 1492
practice.why: Those baptised in 1391 and their descendants became the conversos; suspicion of them led to the Inquisition, and the decree of 1492 blames the 'interaction between the Jews and these Christians'.

wrong.1: The attacks began in Seville; Granada surrendered only in 1492.
wrong.2: Suspicion of the conversos, who were baptised Christians, led to the Inquisition.
wrong.3: Alfonso X died in 1284; the decree came from Ferdinand and Isabella.

pages.title: Timur and the Ottomans
pages.lede: Timur, a conqueror from Central Asia, campaigned from India to Anatolia and strove to make Samarkand the most splendid city in Asia. At Ankara he captured the sultan of a rising Turkish dynasty, the Ottomans, and plunged it into civil war. The Ottomans recovered, and about half a century later took Constantinople, an event still contested in memory.
body: Timur massacred whole cities in Iran and invaded India, [[c-timur]] while striving to make Samarkand, the capital of his realm, the most splendid city in Asia; its monuments of the Timurid age include the Bibi-Khanum mosque, the Gur-Emir mausoleum and Ulugh Beg's observatory. [[c-samarkand]] In 1402 he crushed the Ottomans at Ankara and captured their sultan. [[c-ankara]]

The Ottomans had grown from a small principality in north-western Anatolia into a power on both sides of the Dardanelles. [[c-osman]] Why they grew so fast is debated, [[c-gaza]] but one institution was distinctive: the devshirme, which took Christian boys, converted them and trained them as soldiers and officials. [[c-devsirme]]

On 29 May 1453 Mehmed II took Constantinople, ending the Roman empire in the east. [[c-1453]] He presented himself as heir to the Caesars as well as a champion of Islam. [[c-mehmed]] Hagia Sophia became a mosque, and in 2020 it became one again, to praise and protest. [[c-hagiasophia]]

head: Year
Event
rows: Gallipoli becomes a permanent Ottoman base in Europe

practice.q: What was the immediate consequence of the battle of Ankara (1402) for the Ottomans?
choices: Bayezid was captured and his sons fought a civil war
Timur went on to take Constantinople from the Byzantines
Bayezid defeated Timur and went on to take Samarkand
Timur made Ankara the new capital of his realm
practice.why: Bayezid I, the only Ottoman ruler ever captured by an enemy, was taken, and a civil war among his sons followed until 1413.

wrong.1: Constantinople fell to Mehmed II in 1453.
wrong.2: Timur won; Bayezid was captured.
wrong.3: Samarkand was the capital of Timur's realm.

practice.q: What is the debate over Paul Wittek's 'gaza thesis' about?
choices: Whether holy war drove the early Ottomans' rapid growth
Whether Wittek's critics proved holy war was the main motive
Whether Osman's principality began in north-western Anatolia
Whether Timur's victory at Ankara ended Ottoman expansion
practice.why: Wittek argued the Ottomans were driven by gaza, holy war against Christians; severe criticism from the 1980s left the thesis 'largely undermined'.

wrong.1: The reverse: the critics left Wittek's thesis 'largely undermined'.
wrong.2: That is not in dispute; the debate is about why the Ottomans grew so fast.
wrong.3: The gaza debate concerns the causes of the early growth; after Ankara the Ottomans recovered, and Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453.

pages.title: Africa, 1250 to 1500
pages.lede: Mali's kings grew rich on West African gold, and one of them astonished Cairo on his way to Mecca. Timbuktu became a city of scholars. In the south, Great Zimbabwe and Kilwa flourished on trade, and in Ethiopia a new dynasty claimed descent from Solomon.
body: Mali was founded by Sundiata in the 13th century, [[c-sundiata]] though most of his story comes from an epic that historians use with care. [[c-sunjata-epic]] Its most famous ruler, Mansa Musa, made his pilgrimage in 1324 and spent so much gold in Cairo that its price fell, [[c-musa]] and he built mosques at Gao and Timbuktu. [[c-musa-mosques]] His wealth became legendary. [[c-musa-wealth]]

Timbuktu became one of Islam's great centres of learning. [[c-timbuktu]] Its family libraries survived into the 21st century, and their manuscripts were moved south to Bamako around the time armed groups occupied the city in 2012-13. [[c-timbuktu-mss]] Mali's power passed in the 15th century to Songhay. [[c-songhai]]

In the south, Great Zimbabwe was an important trading centre of the interior, [[c-gz]] and Kilwa a prosperous port on the coast. [[c-kilwa2]] In Ethiopia the Solomonic dynasty took power in 1270, [[c-solomonid]] its claims set out in the Kebra Nagast. [[c-kebra]] On the Atlantic side, the kingdoms of Benin [[c-benin]] and Kongo were growing when the Portuguese arrived. [[c-kongo]]

practice.q: Why do historians use the Sunjata epic with caution as evidence for 13th-century Mali?
choices: It mixes myth with episodes no one has confirmed
It was invented by French officers in the 1880s
Conrad reads it as pure invention with no history
It survives in one fixed version from the 1300s
practice.why: David Conrad: 'Some themes are obviously mythical, while others could have a historical basis but cannot be independently confirmed.'

wrong.1: Ibn Khaldun mentioned Sundiata in the late 14th century; versions of the epic have been recorded since the late 19th century.
wrong.2: Conrad allows that some themes 'could have a historical basis'.
wrong.3: It has been recorded in many versions since the late 19th century.

practice.q: In economic terms, what did Mansa Musa's spending in Cairo in 1324 do?
choices: It flooded Cairo with gold, so gold's value fell
It made gold scarcer in Cairo, so its value rose
It proved Musa the richest person who has ever lived
It kept Mali's gold wealth hidden from outsiders
practice.why: He spent so much gold in Cairo that its value there fell: more supply, lower price.

wrong.1: The reverse: the gold he spent made its value fall.
wrong.2: Claims that he was the wealthiest person who ever lived cannot be checked; no record allows a modern money value.
wrong.3: His wealth became famous; the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows him holding a gold coin.

pages.title: Ming China and East Asia
pages.lede: A peasant rebel drove out the Mongols and founded the Ming dynasty. His son built the Forbidden City and sent great fleets across the Indian Ocean, and then China stopped sending them. In Korea a king invented an alphabet, and in Japan the shoguns' power weakened.
body: The Red Turban rebellion against the Mongols was put down, [[c-redturbans]] but a rival rebel, the peasant-born Zhu Yuanzhang, toppled the Yuan dynasty and founded the Ming in 1368. [[c-hongwu]] His son, the Yongle emperor, seized the throne and moved the capital to Beijing. [[c-yongle]]

Yongle also sent the admiral Zheng He on the first of seven great voyages, [[c-zhenghe]] to display Ming power and draw distant rulers into the tribute system. [[c-zhenghe-why]] How large his ships were is still argued over. [[c-shipsize]] After 1433 the voyages stopped, criticised as too costly. [[c-zhenghe-end]]

In Korea, King Sejong created an alphabet so that ordinary people could write their own language. [[c-hangul]] In Japan the Ashikaga shoguns' power was weak from the outset and weakened further; the Ōnin War broke out in 1467. [[c-ashikaga]]

figure.caption: Ming China and Zheng He's voyages, 1405-1433

practice.q: Why do estimates of the size of Zheng He's largest ships vary so widely?
choices: Texts give 117-149 m, too long for wooden ships, critics say
No Chinese text records the treasure ships' lengths
A complete treasure ship has been excavated and measured
Needham and Levathes judged such ships impossible
practice.why: Chinese texts give lengths of about 117-149 m, but whether wooden ships that big could be built is debated; a 2026 review suggests 60-76 m.

wrong.1: Chinese texts give the largest ships lengths of about 117-149 m.
wrong.2: The debate rests on the texts and on whether such wooden ships could be built.
wrong.3: Needham, Levathes and Dreyer accepted the figures; Sleeswyk, Wake and Church judged them impossible.

practice.q: What reason was given for creating the Korean alphabet?
choices: Chinese characters did not suit writing Korean
Korea needed a script of its own for dealing with the Ming
Korean envoys needed a script for writing Japanese
To give Korean thousands of new characters
practice.why: Chinese characters were not suitable for writing Korean, so common people could not record their thoughts.

wrong.1: The reason given was that common people could not record their thoughts in Chinese characters.
wrong.2: It was made for writing Korean.
wrong.3: It has 28 letters, not thousands of characters.

pages.title: India and the Indian Ocean
pages.lede: The Delhi Sultanate became an imperial power and then broke apart, its power in the north shattered by Timur. New states rose in the south, Hindu Vijayanagara and the Muslim Bahmani sultanate. Along the coasts, ports such as Calicut and Melaka flourished on Indian Ocean trade.
body: The Khalji sultans made Delhi an imperial power. [[c-khaljis]] Muhammad bin Tughluq moved his capital south and experimented with token coins, [[c-tughluq]] and historians still argue over whether he was a visionary or a tyrant. [[c-tughluq-view]] In 1398 Timur's invasion broke the Sultanate's power in the north. [[c-timur-delhi]]
In the Deccan and the south, Vijayanagara [[c-vijayanagara]] and the Bahmani sultanate fought for generations. [[c-bahmani]]

The Indian Ocean linked them all to the wider world. Calicut traded pepper with Arab merchants and received the Chinese fleets, [[c-calicut]] and Melaka, on the strait between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, became the region's greatest market. [[c-melaka]]

practice.q: Which description best fits Muhammad bin Tughluq's token currency?
choices: Base-metal coins with a silver face value
Paper notes copied from those of Yuan China
A successful reform kept by his successors
A plan to move the royal mint to Calicut
practice.why: He issued coins of base metal with the face value of silver, an experiment that 'failed dismally'.

wrong.1: The token currency was coins of base metal, not paper.
wrong.2: It 'failed dismally'.
wrong.3: His move was of the capital, to Daulatabad in the Deccan; the token currency was base-metal coin.

practice.q: What best explains Melaka's rise by the 1430s?
choices: Its strait position and ties with Ming China
Its founding by Portuguese traders around 1400
Its role as the port of Vijayanagara's empire
Timur's conquest, which made it his naval base
practice.why: Melaka lay on the strait between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, and became a tributary of Ming China; by the 1430s it was Southeast Asia's leading emporium.

wrong.1: It was founded around 1400 by Parameswara.
wrong.2: Vijayanagara's capital was Hampi in the south of India; Melaka was a tributary of Ming China.
wrong.3: Timur's invasion struck Delhi in 1398-99.

pages.title: The Americas
pages.sub: the Mexica and the Inca, c. 1325 to 1500
pages.lede: In the 15th century two great empires rose in the Americas, the Mexica (Aztec) in central Mexico and the Inca in the Andes. Both grew rapidly in the 15th century, and both drew tribute from the peoples they conquered.
body: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on a lake in central Mexico, [[c-tenochtitlan]] and after 1428 their Triple Alliance collected tribute across much of Mexico. [[c-triple]] Human sacrifice was commonly practised as part of their religion. [[c-aztec-sacrifice]] The great skull rack found in Mexico City has confirmed it on a large scale, including women and children, [[c-tzompantli]] though the numbers given by Spanish writers are still disputed. [[c-sacrifice-scale]]

In the Andes, Pachacuti began the Inca expansion in the mid-15th century, [[c-pachacuti]] knitting the empire together with roads [[c-qhapaq]] and keeping records on knotted cords that are only beginning to be read. [[c-khipu]] [[c-khipu2025]] Among the peoples the Inca conquered were the Chimú of the Peruvian coast. [[c-chanchan]]
How many people lived in the Americas on the eve of contact is uncertain, [[c-pop1492]] and what happened to them after 1492 is the story of Chapter 13.

practice.q: What have the Huey Tzompantli excavations done to the debate over Aztec sacrifice?
choices: Confirmed mass sacrifice, but not the top Spanish figures
Confirmed Diego Durán's 80,400 victims at one dedication
Shown that sacrifice victims were adult male warriors
Dated the rack to the years after the Spanish conquest
practice.why: Archaeology now confirms sacrifice on a large scale, including women and children, but not the largest Spanish figures.

wrong.1: Archaeology does not confirm the largest Spanish figures, such as Durán's.
wrong.2: Of the skulls studied, 38 percent were women and 2 percent children.
wrong.3: It was built in stages between 1486 and 1502.

practice.q: Which statement about the population of the Americas in 1492 is best supported?
choices: A 2019 synthesis gives 60.5 million, within a wide range
Inca and Mexica censuses give exact totals for both continents
Dobyns's 112 million is now the agreed figure
Recent estimates put it below 20 million people
practice.why: Estimates range from about 54 million (Denevan) to 112 million (Dobyns); Koch et al. (2019) give 60.5 million, with a middle range of 44.8-78.2 million.

wrong.1: Khipus are only beginning to be read: six were matched to a Spanish census of 1670.
wrong.2: Estimates range from about 54 million to 112 million, and a 2019 synthesis gives 60.5 million.
wrong.3: Denevan gives about 54 million and Dobyns 112 million; it was early-20th-century estimates that were much lower.
